The Small Bengal silver-biddy Gerres setifer attains a maximum standard length of 15 centimeters [Li = 15 centimeters], a size that places it among the smaller members of the family Gerreidae. This ultimate length is typically reached within the species' warm-water habitats, where growth trajectories are strongly influenced by local thermal regimes. In contrast, the onset of reproductive capability occurs at a considerably smaller body size, with individuals first exhibiting signs of gonadal maturation at a standard length of approximately 7 centimeters [Lp = approximately 7 centimeters]. This substantial difference between size at puberty and asymptotic size implies a prolonged period of somatic growth following the attainment of sexual maturity, a life-history pattern that is comparatively unusual among small coastal teleosts.

Field surveys and laboratory observations conducted at a stable water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C] have provided detailed insights into the reproductive biology of G. setifer. At this temperature, females exhibit a maximum daily egg production rate of approximately 82 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 82 eggs per day], a rate that is characteristic of modest fecundity relative to other gerreids and is likely tied to the seasonal availability of planktonic food resources in their estuarine environments.

The initial mass at which G. setifer enters the post-hatching phase is remarkably low, with newly emerged yolk-sac larvae weighing approximately 0.00027 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00027 grams]. This minute birth mass, derived from an egg diameter of roughly 0.8 millimeters, is typical of pelagic-spawning gerreids and necessitates a rapid onset of exogenous feeding to sustain early development. As the larvae progress through the metamorphic transition into the juvenile stage and subsequently toward adulthood, somatic growth is accompanied by a considerable increase in tissue mass. At the point of sexual maturation, when individuals reach a standard length of 7 centimeters, the corresponding wet weight at puberty has been estimated at 3.75 grams [Wwp = 3.75 grams], a value that underscores the substantial post-recruitment growth required to achieve reproductive status.

The maximum adult body mass documented for G. setifer is 35.3 grams [Wwi = 35.3 grams], a value that is attained at the species' ultimate standard length of 15 centimeters. This asymptotic mass represents the culmination of a growth trajectory that is heavily influenced by both intrinsic physiological limits and extrinsic environmental conditions, particularly water temperature. The pronounced increase in wet weight from the 3.75 grams [Wwp = 3.75 grams] recorded at puberty to this final adult mass highlights a prolonged period of post-maturational somatic investment, during which individuals continue to add considerable body tissue before reaching their maximal size.

Longevity records for G. setifer, gathered from individuals maintained under controlled laboratory conditions at a constant temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years]. This modest lifespan is broadly consistent with values reported for other small-bodied gerreid species inhabiting similar tropical and subtropical coastal environments. The combination of a mean daily egg production rate of 82 eggs per day [Ri = 82 eggs per day] and a typical lifespan of 6 years [am = 6 years] suggests that a single female can produce a substantial total number of offspring over her lifetime, though this potential is constrained by resource availability and predation pressure, making local populations potentially vulnerable to overfishing at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C].
